description: We are a multidisciplinary team combining space science, healthcare, AI, and software development. Our project aims to create an intelligent system that monitors astronauts’ vital signs, detects potential health risks, and provides timely alerts during space missions. Through innovation and teamwork, we hope to support astronaut safety and contribute to healthier, more sustainable human space exploration.
summary: Beyond Earth orbit, help is minutes away: on a Mars mission, a medical question to Earth can take up to 20 minutes each way, so the crew must recognize problems on board. Astro Vitals, developed by team Space Health Pioneers, is an explainable health monitoring engine that turns raw wearable readings into a clear status (GREEN, AMBER, RED or GRAY) with a reason in plain English. Because microgravity changes what is “normal” (fluid shifts toward the head, space anemia, a higher resting body temperature), Earth-based cutoffs would trigger constant false alarms. Astro Vitals compares each astronaut with their own in-flight baseline, keeps clinical safety limits as a safety net, escalates when several signals worsen together, and flags unreliable sensor data as GRAY instead of raising a false medical alert.
details:
The problem

On deep-space missions, communication delays and the lack of a hospital mean the crew must detect health problems on board. Existing clinical alarm systems were designed for hospital patients on Earth: in microgravity, an astronaut’s normal heart rate, blood volume and body temperature shift, so fixed terrestrial cutoffs either miss early changes or flood the crew with false alarms. A loose sensor can also look like an emergency.

What Astro Vitals does

Astro Vitals is a rule-based engine that analyzes heart rate, SpO₂, respiratory rate, systolic blood pressure and core temperature and returns one of four states: GREEN (normal), AMBER (watch), RED (urgent) or GRAY (unreliable data). Every result states what changed, compared to what, and for how long, along with the rule that fired.

How it works

Readings pass through five stages: validate, quality gate, personal baseline, detect and explain.

• Data quality gate: low sensor quality, impossible values, stale data, flat-lined sensors, impossible jumps and isolated spikes are marked GRAY. They are never shown as a medical alert or as a falsely reassuring GREEN.

• Two detection layers in parallel, the more severe one wins: a personal baseline (robust z-score of 2 or more from the astronaut’s own median, or an SpO₂ drop of 4 points) gives early AMBER warnings, while fixed limits derived from the clinical early-warning score NEWS2 act as a safety net. RED requires 15 seconds of valid data and AMBER bands 5 minutes, which filters out momentary noise.

• Advisories: mild changes, such as SpO₂ of 94% or a slight temperature rise, prompt a sensor check without raising an alarm.

• Multi-signal escalation to RED: two signals in amber for 10 minutes (MS-01), low SpO₂ with rising respiratory rate, a possible respiratory problem or CO₂ build-up (MS-02), an amber signal plus a reported symptom (MS-04), or a combined early-warning score of 5 or more (MS-05).

• Mission phases: during days 1–7, while the body adapts to microgravity, only fixed limits are active. The personal baseline becomes provisional on day 8 and stable from day 22. From day 8, core temperature uses in-flight limits shifted upward, because resting body temperature rises in space.

Tools and validation

Python, with all thresholds in a single versioned JSON configuration file so a medical team can adjust them without touching the code, and pytest for testing. The engine passes 93 automated tests that check every threshold at its exact boundary, a fuzz test of 1,500 random and malformed inputs with no crash, and a stress test of 300 simulated crew members with zero misclassifications across four scenarios (normal day, single-signal watch, multi-signal deterioration and sensor failure). The output is JSON, ready for a dashboard.

Scientific basis

Every threshold and design choice is traced to the team’s biomedical research report and alert threshold specification, built on the NASA Human Research Program, Canadian Space Agency research (Bio-Monitor, CARDIOBREATH) and NEWS2, plus a sleep and fatigue research report.

Why it is different

Most monitoring tools compare everyone with the same range. Astro Vitals adapts to each astronaut, keeps detected sensor faults separate from real illness, and explains every alert instead of producing a black-box score, so the crew can trust and act on it without waiting for Earth.

Limitations and next steps

All data is synthetic, because real-time astronaut vitals are not public, and the NEWS2-based limits are a prototype that requires medical review before real use. Next, we plan an exercise mode using the rate-pressure product to detect cardiac strain during workouts (MS-07), a multi-day HRV and sleep trend rule for fatigue (MS-03), and testing on public wearable datasets.

Impact beyond space

The same approach (a personal baseline, transparent rules and sensor-fault detection) can support remote and rural patient monitoring and wearable early warning on Earth, where specialists are far away.
